conflicts.name: The Fourth Crusade and the sack of Constantinople
conflicts.religionRoleNote: The expedition was called by Pope Innocent III in 1198 as a penitential war to recover Jerusalem, and its participants took the cross and the crusade indulgence. Its diversion first to Zara and then to Constantinople was driven chiefly by debt to Venice, the ambitions of the Byzantine pretender Alexios Angelos, Venetian commercial interests and the logistics of a stranded army. Religion re-entered decisively at the end: clergy in the camp told the troops in April 1204 that the Greeks were schismatic ‘enemies of God’ and that the assault was just and meritorious. Older ‘conspiracy’ theories (a plot by Venice or the Hohenstaufen) have largely given way to the ‘accident’ or ‘series of contingencies’ view of Queller and Madden, though Angold and Phillips stress how long-standing Latin–Greek antagonism made the outcome thinkable.

sides.name: Crusader army and the Republic of Venice
Byzantine Empire
leaders: Isaac II and Alexios IV Angelos (restored by the crusaders)

sides.name: Zara (Zadar) and the Kingdom of Hungary

conflicts.summary: A crusade launched by Innocent III to strike at Ayyubid Egypt never reached the Muslim world. Unable to pay Venice for its fleet, the army sacked the Catholic city of Zara in 1202, then backed a Byzantine pretender, and in April 1204 stormed and plundered Constantinople, the greatest Christian city of the age. A Latin Empire was set up in its place. The sack hardened the schism between Latin and Orthodox Christians for centuries.
conflicts.story:
In August 1198 the newly elected Innocent III issued the bull Post miserabile calling for a new crusade after the failure of the Third Crusade to recover Jerusalem. Northern French nobles took the cross at the tournament of Écry in November 1199, and their envoys, including the chronicler Geoffrey of Villehardouin, contracted with Venice in April 1201 for ships and supplies for 33,500 men at a price of 85,000 marks; the secret strategic aim was Egypt, the heart of Ayyubid power. When the leader, Count Thibaut of Champagne, died in 1201, command passed to Boniface, marquis of Montferrat, whose family had close ties to Byzantium.

By the summer of 1202 only about a third of the expected army had gathered at Venice, and it could not pay its debt. The aged, nearly blind doge Enrico Dandolo, who took the cross himself in St Mark’s, offered a postponement in return for help in recovering Zara (Zadar) on the Dalmatian coast, which had rebelled against Venice and placed itself under the Catholic king of Hungary, himself a crusader. Despite a papal prohibition, read out in the camp by Abbot Guy of Vaux-de-Cernay, the army besieged and sacked Zara in November 1202. Innocent excommunicated the whole host; he later absolved the French crusaders but not the Venetians.

At Zara envoys arrived from the young Alexios Angelos, son of the deposed emperor Isaac II, who promised 200,000 marks, 10,000 troops for the crusade, the maintenance of 500 knights in the Holy Land and the submission of the Greek Church to Rome if the crusaders restored his father. Many crusaders left in protest, but the majority sailed via Corfu and reached Constantinople in June 1203. After an assault on 17 July 1203 the usurper Alexios III fled; Isaac II was restored with his son crowned as co-emperor Alexios IV. A fire started by crusaders attacking a mosque in August 1203 destroyed a large swathe of the city.

Alexios IV could not raise the promised money, and Byzantine hostility to the Latins grew. In late January 1204 he was overthrown and in February strangled by Alexios V Doukas (‘Mourtzouphlos’), who refused to honour the agreement. In March the crusaders and Venetians agreed in advance how to divide the empire. The clergy in the camp assured the troops that the Greeks, as schismatics who had murdered their lord, were enemies of God and that those who died in the attack would gain the crusade indulgence. A first assault on 9 April failed; on 12 April the walls along the Golden Horn were breached.

For three days Constantinople was sacked. Churches and monasteries were looted, nuns assaulted and the holy places desecrated; the Byzantine historian Niketas Choniates, who escaped with his family, described soldiers stripping the altar of Hagia Sophia and a prostitute seated on the patriarch’s throne. A great part of the city’s treasure and relics was carried West, among them the bronze horses now at St Mark’s in Venice and countless relics brought to French and German churches. The number killed is unknown; contemporaries stress plunder and rape more than mass slaughter, but the fires of 1203–1204 left much of the city in ruins.

Baldwin of Flanders was crowned Latin emperor in Hagia Sophia on 16 May 1204, and the Venetian Thomas Morosini became Latin patriarch. The Latin Empire never controlled more than part of Byzantium: Greek successor states arose at Nicaea, in Epirus and at Trebizond, and in April 1205 the Bulgarian tsar Kaloyan crushed the Latins at Adrianople and captured Baldwin, who died in captivity. Michael VIII Palaiologos of Nicaea recovered Constantinople in 1261, but the restored empire was poorer and weaker. Innocent III, who had welcomed the conquest at first as a providential reunion of the churches, wrote in 1205 that the Greeks now had reason to detest the Latins ‘more than dogs’.
conflicts.nameOfGod: The army marched under the crusade vow and the plenary indulgence granted by Innocent III for the recovery of the Holy Land. At Zara and again before Constantinople the bishops in the camp, including the bishops of Soissons and Troyes, preached that attacking the Greeks was licit because they had broken from Rome and killed their emperor, and promised the indulgence to those who fell. Looting of relics was justified by some, such as Abbot Martin of Pairis, as a holy theft (furta sacra) bringing sacred objects into more worthy hands.
religiousCauses: Innocent III’s call in 1198 for a new crusade to recover Jerusalem, lost to Saladin in 1187, provided the original purpose and the indulgence.
Long-standing Latin suspicion of the Greek Church, sharpened since 1054 and by the massacre of Latins in Constantinople in 1182, made the Byzantines seem unreliable or even hostile to the crusade.
Alexios Angelos’s promise to bring the Greek Church under papal obedience gave the diversion a religious justification in Western eyes.
The clergy in the camp presented the assault of 1204 as a just war against schismatics and regicides, promising the indulgence to the attackers.
otherCauses: The crusaders’ inability to pay Venice the 85,000 marks owed under the treaty of 1201, because far fewer men came to Venice than had been planned.
Venetian commercial and strategic interests in the Adriatic and in Byzantine trade, and resentment over the Byzantine arrest of Venetians in 1171.
The Angelos family’s dynastic quarrel, which offered the crusaders money and troops for restoring Isaac II and his son.
Western ideas, voiced since the Second and Third Crusades, that Byzantium had obstructed earlier crusades and that its wealth could fund a new one.
The breakdown of relations after Alexios IV failed to pay and was murdered, leaving the army without supplies in a hostile land.
triggers: The deal of autumn 1202 by which Dandolo offered to defer the debt in return for the capture of Zara.
Alexios Angelos’s offer, received at Zara in January 1203, to pay and reunite the churches if his father were restored.
The murder of Alexios IV by Alexios V Doukas in February 1204, which ended any hope of payment and was presented as regicide.

timeline.text: Innocent III proclaims a new crusade in the bull Post miserabile.
French nobles take the cross at the tournament of Écry in Champagne.
Treaty of Venice: the Republic agrees to transport 33,500 crusaders for 85,000 marks; Boniface of Montferrat becomes leader.
The underfunded army sails from Venice and sacks Catholic Zara in November, defying a papal ban; Innocent excommunicates the host.
Crusaders reach Constantinople, drive out Alexios III and restore Isaac II with Alexios IV; a great fire ravages the city in August.
Alexios IV is murdered in February; on 12–15 April the crusaders storm and sack Constantinople; Baldwin of Flanders is crowned Latin emperor in May.
Tsar Kaloyan of Bulgaria defeats the Latins at Adrianople and captures Baldwin; Innocent III condemns the crusaders’ conduct.
Michael VIII Palaiologos recovers Constantinople and ends the Latin Empire.
Pope John Paul II, in Athens, asks God’s forgiveness for Catholic sins against the Orthodox, naming the sack of Constantinople.
On the 800th anniversary John Paul II expresses ‘pain and disgust’ at the sack to Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew, who accepts the apology.

keyPeople.name: Innocent III
keyPeople.focus: Called the crusade, forbade attacks on Christians and excommunicated the army after Zara, but did not stop the diversion and initially welcomed the Latin Empire.
keyPeople.outcome: Later condemned the sack in letters of 1205; went on to call the Albigensian Crusade and the Fifth Crusade.

keyPeople.name: Enrico Dandolo
keyPeople.focus: Negotiated the transport treaty, proposed the attack on Zara and led the Venetian fleet in the assaults on Constantinople despite near blindness.
keyPeople.outcome: Died in Constantinople in 1205 and was buried in Hagia Sophia; Venice gained ‘a quarter and half of a quarter’ of the empire and key ports.

keyPeople.name: Boniface of Montferrat
keyPeople.focus: Accepted the alliance with Alexios Angelos and led the army to Constantinople.
keyPeople.outcome: Passed over for the imperial crown; became king of Thessalonica and was killed fighting the Bulgarians in 1207.

keyPeople.name: Baldwin I of Constantinople (Baldwin IX of Flanders)
keyPeople.focus: Commanded a division in the assaults and was elected emperor after the sack.
keyPeople.outcome: Captured by Kaloyan at Adrianople in 1205 and died in Bulgarian captivity.

keyPeople.name: Alexios IV Angelos
keyPeople.focus: Offered money, troops and church union for the crusaders’ help in restoring his father.
keyPeople.outcome: Unable to pay, he was deposed and strangled in February 1204.

keyPeople.name: Alexios V Doukas ‘Mourtzouphlos’
keyPeople.focus: Seized power, organised the defence of the city and refused to pay the crusaders.
keyPeople.outcome: Fled before the final assault; captured and executed by the Latins by being thrown from the Column of Theodosius.

keyPeople.name: Geoffrey of Villehardouin
keyPeople.focus: Negotiated the Venetian treaty and later wrote The Conquest of Constantinople, defending the leaders’ decisions.
keyPeople.outcome: Became marshal of Romania; his chronicle is a principal Western source.

keyPeople.name: Niketas Choniates
keyPeople.focus: Witnessed the sack and escaped with his family; his History records it in detail.
keyPeople.outcome: Died in exile at Nicaea; his lament is the key Greek account of 1204.

casualties.note: No reliable figures exist for deaths in the sieges and sack of 1203–1204. Choniates and Western chroniclers stress looting, rape and desecration rather than mass killing, and modern historians (Phillips, Angold) do not offer a total; some suggest civilian deaths in the low thousands, but this is an inference. The fires of 1203–1204 destroyed large districts and displaced many thousands. Losses at Zara and in the 1205 defeat at Adrianople are likewise unquantified.

effects: The Byzantine Empire was dismembered into a Latin Empire, Venetian possessions, Frankish principalities in Greece and Greek successor states at Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond.
Venice gained a maritime empire of ports and islands, including Crete, that underpinned its commercial power for centuries.
The restored Byzantine state after 1261 was much weaker, which eased the later Ottoman advance into the Balkans and the fall of Constantinople in 1453.
An immense transfer of relics, art and treasure to the West, including the horses of St Mark’s and many relics later housed in Western churches.
No help reached the Latin East, and the crusading movement began to be redirected against Christian targets.
effectsOnChurch: The sack is widely regarded as the moment the schism of 1054 became a lasting popular estrangement between Orthodox and Latin Christians.

Latin patriarchs and bishops were imposed in Constantinople and Greece, giving the Orthodox a lived experience of forced ‘union’ that coloured later reunion attempts at Lyon (1274) and Florence (1439).
Western piety was reshaped by the flood of relics, including relics of the Passion later acquired by Louis IX for the Sainte-Chapelle.
In 2001 and 2004 Pope John Paul II apologised for the sack, and Patriarch Bartholomew accepted the apology, a milestone in Catholic–Orthodox reconciliation.
conflicts.legacy: The Fourth Crusade became the classic example of a crusade turned against fellow Christians and of religious language serving money and power. For Orthodox Christians it remains a deep historical wound, invoked in debates about union with Rome; for historians it is a case study in how a sequence of financial and political decisions, rather than a single plot, could carry a holy war to an unholy end.

dissenters.name: Guy, abbot of Vaux-de-Cernay
dissenters.text: A Cistercian in the army, he read out Innocent III’s letter forbidding an attack on Zara and declared that Christians must not be attacked; he left the army rather than go on to Constantinople.

dissenters.name: Simon de Montfort
dissenters.text: Refused to take part in the siege of Zara and left the crusade with his followers to sail independently to the Holy Land; he later led the Albigensian Crusade.

dissenters.name: Innocent III
dissenters.text: Forbade the attacks on Christians, excommunicated the army after Zara, and in 1205 rebuked his legate and the crusaders for the sack, writing that it had made the Greek Church detest the Latins.

dissenters.name: Niketas Choniates
dissenters.text: The Orthodox historian condemned the crusaders as men who ‘bore the cross on their shoulders’ yet behaved worse than the Saracens, who had spared Jerusalem in 1187.

theatres.name: Galata Tower and the Golden Horn chain

campaigns.title: From Venice to Constantinople
campaigns.people: The crusade army and the Venetian fleet under Boniface of Montferrat and Enrico Dandolo
campaigns.text: The fleet left Venice in October 1202, wintered at Zara after sacking it, and in spring 1203 sailed with Alexios Angelos via Durazzo and Corfu, through the Dardanelles to the Asian shore opposite Constantinople, which it attacked in July 1203 and stormed in April 1204.

conflicts.name: Later crusades to the East: Damietta, Frederick II, Louis IX and the fall of Acre
conflicts.religionRoleNote: These expeditions were preached as penitential wars for the recovery and defence of Jerusalem and the Holy Land, funded by church taxes and rewarded with the plenary indulgence; for leaders such as Louis IX, personal piety was plainly the driving motive. Historians in the ‘pluralist’ school (Riley-Smith, Housley) stress the sincerity of crusading devotion, while others (Tyerman) emphasise how papal finance, dynastic prestige, Italian commerce and the papacy’s parallel crusades against Christian rulers such as Frederick II blurred the ideal. On the Muslim side the Ayyubids and Mamluks also framed the struggle as jihad, especially under Baybars.

sides.name: Crusaders and the Latin East
leaders: the Templars, Hospitallers and Teutonic Knights
